reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: The mandible commonly fractures at more than one site because of its arch shape, so a fracture at one point should prompt a search for a second, often contralateral, fracture such as the condyle
Malocclusion, a change in the patient's usual bite, is a sensitive sign of mandibular fracture and must be specifically asked about and examined
Other clinical signs include pain on jaw movement, trismus, a step in the dental arch, sublingual haematoma, and numbness of the lower lip from inferior alveolar nerve injury
Panoramic radiography and CT are used to define fracture site, displacement, and the relationship to tooth roots and the inferior alveolar nerve
Fractures involving tooth-bearing bone communicate with the mouth and are effectively open, requiring antibiotics and timely management to reduce infection risk
Restoring the pre-injury occlusion is the central goal, achieved with maxillomandibular fixation and/or open reduction with internal fixation depending on the pattern
Many condylar fractures, particularly in children and minimally displaced cases, can be managed conservatively with a short period of fixation and early mobilisation to avoid ankylosis
Bilateral anterior (parasymphyseal) fractures can allow the tongue and anterior segment to fall backward and threaten the airway
reference.pathophysiology: The mandible is a mobile, U-shaped bone whose weaker regions - the condylar neck, angle (often at an unerupted third molar), and parasymphysis - are prone to fracture. Because it forms a ring-like structure articulating at both temporomandibular joints, force at one point is frequently transmitted to produce a second fracture elsewhere. Displacement is influenced by the pull of the muscles of mastication, which can distract or override fracture segments depending on their orientation (favourable versus unfavourable patterns). Fractures through tooth-bearing segments breach the oral mucosa, creating a contaminated, effectively open injury, and disruption of the inferior alveolar nerve within the canal causes lower lip and chin numbness.
additionalDifferentials: Dentoalveolar fracture or isolated dental trauma
Zygomatic or midface fracture causing trismus
Pathological fracture through a cyst or tumour
Temporomandibular joint dysfunction unrelated to trauma
additionalInvestigations: Panoramic radiograph (orthopantomogram) as an initial survey of the mandible
CT for detailed assessment of condyle, displacement, and comminution
Careful occlusal and dental examination to detect malocclusion and tooth injury
Inferior alveolar nerve sensory testing of the lower lip and chin
Assessment for a second fracture given the ring anatomy of the mandible
redFlags: Airway compromise from bilateral parasymphyseal fractures with posterior displacement of the tongue (emergency)
Displaced open fracture through tooth-bearing bone with infection risk
Signs of associated cervical spine or head injury in high-energy trauma
Progressive infection or abscess from an untreated open mandibular fracture
reference.prognosis: Most mandibular fractures heal well with restored occlusion and function when reduction and fixation are appropriate, and many condylar fractures do well with conservative management. Poorer outcomes - malunion, malocclusion, nonunion, infection, temporomandibular joint stiffness or ankylosis, and persistent nerve numbness - are associated with delayed treatment, inadequate reduction, open contaminated fractures, or prolonged immobilisation.
pitfalls: Missing a second (often condylar) fracture after identifying the first
Failing to recognise malocclusion as a key diagnostic sign
Underestimating infection risk in fractures communicating with the oral cavity
Overlooking airway risk in bilateral anterior fractures
Prolonged rigid immobilisation of condylar fractures leading to stiffness or ankylosis
Neglecting to document inferior alveolar nerve deficit before intervention
